title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 15
paragraphs: "My dear Boris," said Princess Anna Mikhaylovna to her son as Countess Rostova's carriage, in which they were riding, rolled over the straw-covered street and turned into the wide courtyard of Count Kirill Vladimirovich Bezukhov's mansion. "My dear Boris," said the mother, drawing her hand from beneath her old cloak and laying it timidly and tenderly on her son's arm, "be warm and attentive to him. Count Kirill Vladimirovich is your godfather, after all, and your future depends on him. Remember that, my dear, and be as charming as you know how to be."
"If I thought anything besides humiliation would come of it..." her son replied coldly. "But I promised, and I'll do it for your sake."

Although the hall porter could see someone's carriage standing at the entrance, after sizing up the mother and son — who had walked straight through the glass vestibule between the rows of statues in niches without asking to be announced — and casting a meaningful look at the lady's old cloak, he asked whether they wanted to see the count or the princesses. When he heard they wished to see the count, he said his excellency was worse today and was not receiving anyone.
"[Speaking in French] We might as well go back," said the son.
"My dear!" his mother exclaimed imploringly, laying her hand on his arm again as if that touch could both soothe and strengthen him.
Boris said nothing more but looked at his mother questioningly, without removing his cloak.

"My friend," Anna Mikhaylovna said gently, addressing the hall porter, "I know Count Kirill Vladimirovich is very ill... that's exactly why I've come. I'm a relative. I won't disturb him, my friend... I only need to see Prince Vasili Sergeevich — he's staying here, isn't he? Please announce me."
The hall porter sullenly pulled a bell that rang upstairs and turned away.

"Princess Drubetskaya to see Prince Vasili Sergeevich," he called to a footman dressed in knee breeches, buckled shoes, and a tailcoat, who came running down the stairs and peered over from the halfway landing.
The mother smoothed the folds of her faded silk dress in front of a large Venetian mirror on the wall and, in her worn-down shoes, briskly climbed the carpeted staircase.
"My dear," she said to her son, rallying him once more with a touch, "you promised me!"
The son, lowering his eyes, followed her quietly.
They entered the large hall, from which one of the doors led to Prince Vasili's apartments.

Just as the mother and son reached the middle of the hall and were about to ask directions from an elderly footman who had jumped up when they entered, the bronze handle of one of the doors turned and Prince Vasili emerged — wearing a velvet coat with a single star on his chest, as he always did at home — saying goodbye to a good-looking, dark-haired man. This was the celebrated Petersburg doctor, Lorrain.
"So it's certain?" said the prince.
"Prince, to err is human, but..." replied the doctor, swallowing his r's and pronouncing the Latin words with a French accent.
The original Latin footnote: To err is human.
"Very well, very well..."

Seeing Anna Mikhaylovna and her son, Prince Vasili dismissed the doctor with a bow and approached them silently, with a questioning look. The son noticed that a look of deep sorrow suddenly crossed his mother's face, and he smiled faintly.
"Ah, Prince! What sad circumstances bring us together again! And how is our dear patient?" she said, as though unaware of the cold, hostile stare directed at her.

Prince Vasili looked at her and at Boris, puzzled and wary. Boris bowed politely. Prince Vasili, without acknowledging the bow, turned to Anna Mikhaylovna and answered her question with a movement of his head and lips that indicated very little hope for the patient.
"Is it possible?" Anna Mikhaylovna exclaimed. "Oh, how terrible! It's dreadful to think... This is my son," she added, indicating Boris. "He wanted to thank you personally."
Boris bowed politely again.
"Believe me, Prince, a mother's heart will never forget what you've done for us."

"I'm glad I was able to be of service, my dear Anna Mikhaylovna," said Prince Vasili, adjusting his lace cravat. His tone and manner here in Moscow, with Anna Mikhaylovna whom he had placed under an obligation, carried far more self-importance than it had at Anna Pavlovna's reception in Petersburg.
"Try to serve well and show yourself worthy," he added, turning to Boris with severity. "I'm glad... Are you here on leave?" he went on, reverting to his usual tone of indifference.

"I'm awaiting orders to join my new regiment, your excellency," Boris replied, showing neither annoyance at the prince's curt manner nor eagerness to engage in conversation, but speaking so quietly and respectfully that the prince gave him a searching look.
"Are you living with your mother?"
"I'm staying with Countess Rostova," Boris replied, again adding, "your excellency."
"That is, with Ilya Rostov, who married Natalia Shinshina," Anna Mikhaylovna clarified.

"I know, I know," Prince Vasili answered in his monotonous voice. "I could never understand how Natalia brought herself to marry that uncouth bear! A perfectly absurd and stupid man, and a gambler too, I'm told."

"But a very kind man, Prince," said Anna Mikhaylovna with a sympathetic smile, as though she too knew Count Rostov deserved the criticism but was asking the prince not to be too hard on the poor old fellow. "What do the doctors say?" she asked after a pause, her worn face once again expressing deep sorrow.
"They give little hope," replied the prince.
"And I did so want to thank Uncle for all his kindness to me and Boris. He is Boris's godfather," she added, her tone implying that this fact should give Prince Vasili considerable satisfaction.
Prince Vasili grew thoughtful and frowned. Anna Mikhaylovna could see he was afraid of finding a rival for Count Bezukhov's fortune, and she hurried to reassure him.

"If it weren't for my sincere affection and devotion to Uncle," she said — pronouncing the word with studied confidence and nonchalance — "I know his character: noble, upright... but you see, he has no one with him except the young princesses... They're still young..." She lowered her head and continued in a whisper: "Has he fulfilled his final duty, Prince? How precious those last moments are! It can't make things any worse, and he absolutely must be prepared, if he's so ill. We women, Prince," and she smiled tenderly, "always know how to say these things. I simply must see him, however painful it may be for me. I'm accustomed to suffering."
Clearly the prince understood her, just as he had understood at Anna Pavlovna's, that it would be very difficult to get rid of Anna Mikhaylovna.
"Wouldn't such a visit be too much for him, dear Anna Mikhaylovna?" he said. "Let's wait until this evening. The doctors are expecting a crisis."
"But one cannot delay at a moment like this, Prince! Think — the welfare of his soul is at stake. Oh, it's terrible: the duties of a Christian..."

A door from one of the inner rooms opened and one of the princesses — the count's niece — came in with a cold, stern face. Her disproportionately long torso contrasted strikingly with her short legs. Prince Vasili turned to her.
"Well, how is he?"
"The same. But what do you expect, with all this noise..." said the princess, looking at Anna Mikhaylovna as though she were a stranger.

"Ah, my dear, I hardly recognized you," said Anna Mikhaylovna with a bright smile, bustling cheerfully up to the count's niece. "I've come, and I'm here to help you nurse my uncle. I can only imagine what you've been through," she added, turning up her eyes sympathetically.

The princess said nothing, didn't even smile, and left the room. Anna Mikhaylovna removed her gloves and, having claimed her position, settled into an armchair and invited Prince Vasili to sit beside her.

"Boris," she said to her son with a smile, "I'm going in to see the count — my uncle. But you, my dear, should go find Pierre in the meantime. And don't forget to give him the Rostovs' dinner invitation. I don't suppose he'll come?" she added, turning to the prince.

"On the contrary," replied the prince, who had plainly grown gloomy, "I'd be only too grateful if you could take that young man off my hands... He's been here all this time, and the count hasn't asked for him once."
He shrugged. A footman led Boris down one flight of stairs and up another to Pierre's rooms.
